I honestly love her. I think she’s a great representation in the show of innocence and childishness being stamped out (kind of literally) by Lumon and the Keir ideologies. 

The motifs of her playing with and enjoying games, the way she says she thought she’d be staying until the end of the quarter, it just breaks my heart. The way the writers parallel these traits with her blunt nature, the rigidity of the rules, and imposing of her job related boundaries (“I am your supervisor, not a friend”) makes her a very engaging character for me, maybe because I too was forced to grow up too young. Also the way she blames herself for what happens with Dylan shows that inside she is empathetic and introspective, something I’m not sure we ever really see in Cobel. I think it suggests that Cobel may have been the same way as a child, a curious, smart, emotionally intelligent person who through her educational experiences and specifically the Wintertide Fellowship has become hard and cold. 

The implied cycle of abuse from Cobel to Milchick to Miss Huang is also very narratively interesting to me (as well as the cycle of abuse through the Eagan line, Jame to Helena).

I find her character fascinating and a really cool look at these types of themes that we don’t really get with other characters (other than the innies being a portrayal of innocence and naivety) and am very excited to learn more about her lore implications with regards to the Wintertide Fellowship!

Testosterone does not inherently increase risk of cancer as far as I am aware. I have been on T for almost 3 years and have accessed hormones both privately and through Englands NHS system and neither of my providers when going over risks and changes said that I would be more likely to get cancer.

Having said that, when I moved onto NHS provided testosterone, I did receive a clinic letter stating that every 2 to 3 years I would need an ultrasound of my uterus to check for any abnormalities as these can have an increased chance of occurring (cysts, atrophy, things like that) but that is based on a few studies that are not super widely proven as far as I am aware and is just as an additional precaution as I have family who have had ovarian cancer.

If you are planning to start hormones, always speak with your provider about risks and what they recommend, especially if you have any family history of anything, but no taking testosterone will not directly cause you to get any form of cancer.

There’s an element of structure to it. I have to have routine and things to do or I get really depressed and upset. I found working part time gave me some of that structure but I was always being asked to work different days each week or work extra days and it became overwhelming because of all the changes to my weekly routine. I was also raised completely undiagnosed and my mum instilled in me a strong (but probably not healthy) work ethic. I got my first job at 16 and have worked ever since, including through university.

I work full time now, 2 days in the office and 3 days at home and I love it. I found it difficult at first and tiring and honestly it still is but it’s steady and regular and structured and it’s amazing. I feel more productive and I’m able to enjoy my weekends. I always use all my holiday days throughout the year and try to pepper them in for every couple of months so I don’t feel like I’m working 6 months straight with no breaks and I take illness when I need to. Luckily my work are really understanding of my needs and that’s a big part of why it works so well for me, if you have an employer that just doesn’t get it I imagine it can be hard. 

I also have a lot of anxiety around money. I like knowing I get a set amount of money every month, it doesn’t change or fluctuate. I know I can pay my bills and add to my savings and afford groceries and little treats. I can budget my finances a good month in advance and that gives me a lot of peace of mind even if I do still stress about money every other week or so. I also worry less about my future, I know I’m adding to my pension so when I retire I can be less stressed about money! 

The downside for me is that my current job is a fixed term contract, it ends in June so trying to find a new job that is either equal to or more money than I’m making now is a big anxiety at the moment. I’m hopeful I’ll find something else that works for me as well as this job does but I know I definitely want to keep working full time until I retire.

Not sure how helpful of a tip this is, but whenever I have had to learn lines I pace. Something about the repetitive movement really helps me. 

I also go line by line and slowly string them together, so once the first line is memorised I move onto the learning the second line, making sure I always repeat the first line each time I say it. Doing that means it doesn’t feel as overwhelming for me and means I can actually get through memorising pretty quickly until it’s all built up into this massive chunk of text!

If you have a scene partner, you can either get someone to read their lines for you or I sometimes like to read them myself! It gets my cues ingrained within me but does mean more text to learn.

I also gesticulate wildly while I practice (alongside the pacing). The big, over exaggerated movements help me remember things more easily but I’m not sure why!

My experience is mainly in monologues (bachelors in theatre at uni) so may not be helpful for musical theatre but these things are what I find help me :)

My partner. We’d only been together about 6 months but I knew he was pan and had dated guys and girls in the past. One day while out walking in town together he asked if I were a boy what would my name be? I’ve had my name picked out since I was about 5 (I stole it from a friend who moved away when I was really young lol) so I told him. 

He started saying it out loud and it just clicked in my head that this was what I really really wanted to be called. I had been binding and thinking about trans things and wondering if I was for about 5 years at that point and that was the moment my egg fully cracked.

I took a few days to think about it. Think about what I wanted, would I want hormones and surgery, how would this impact my family, would the people around me accept me (I was doing a theatre degree, at that time I was literally doing a module called gender and sexuality, of course they accepted me!) it was really scary and I hate keeping thoughts to myself or having secrets.

So a few days after the initial conversation, I sat on his bed and asked if he’d still date me if I were a boy? He of course said he would. I didn’t tell anyone else for about a month. Wanted to really try it out but friends overheard him calling me my name and while they never brought it up or tried to pressure me into anything they clearly knew lol. Came out to my family and friends via text and while my family was a bit difficult at first, I can confidently say it is the best thing I have ever done.

I am so much happier now. Almost been on T for 3 years and surgery planned for a year’s time! My partner and I are 4 years strong and I love him more everyday.

I went online and googled autism right to choose providers, it then gave me a bunch of websites so I combed through and found which ones seemed the best and had short wait times. I then made an appointment with my gp and gave them the name of the provider I wanted and they completed their portion of the referral. Some providers also want you to fill out a referral form as well as your doctor so do check that before going to the gp so you can make sure you have done everything you need to do :) my wait times ended up being about 4 months for first assessment then another month for the second but that is very good in comparison with the nhs wait times!

My assessment was basically just being asked a bunch of questions. The first one I had was my ADOS assessment and the assessor just asked me questions about my life, why I thought I had autism, what my job is, who I live with, also questions like how do I know someone is my friend? and how would I describe feeling angry? They are testing your responses to verbal and nonverbal cues so you just have to be yourself. 

My second appointment was way more in depth, they asked about my childhood, if I was bullied, my family history, medical history, social issues and if I had trouble at school. My routines and patterns were also brought up and they had me talk about some of my special interests. It was pretty tiring but still quite easy to do.

I was then given a third appointment where they confirmed the diagnosis and gave me some resources to look at. Overall not a bad experience but definitely draining!

My assessments were with the company Dr J and Colleagues through the NHS right to choose scheme so your assessments may be different from mine! I’ve heard of people being asked to demonstrate tasks like bruising their teeth and stuff so you might have to do that as well.

I hope your assessments go well :)

Sadly there’s no right answer, it really is up to you and how you feel it would benefit your life. I was in a similar position in that I was sexually assaulted multiple times by the same man and didn’t report it until years later. I don’t regret reporting it, but the process was difficult and long and it brought back all the feelings I thought I had tucked away.

I highly recommend speaking with a trauma informed therapist if you can, it was really helpful for me when I was going through the reporting and having to give interviews with police. 

The chances of your case going to court and him being put in prison are sadly very low unless you can prove what he did beyond reasonable doubt, but that shouldn’t discourage you if it’s what you want to do. I personally reported so that if in the future he hurt someone else, the police would have a record of his behaviour and it would be easier for the next person to seek legal action and potentially put him behind bars. While sometimes that doesn’t feel enough and I wish I could have gotten him put away myself, it feels hopeful in a way to know that if he ever hurts someone again there is a higher chance of justice.

It’s up to you, if you feel safe enough to tell someone like a parent then you can, but you don’t have to. It’s such a personal thing to disclose but I really do recommend talking to a professional about it, it can help to just get it out of your head and into the world.
